items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The only code is inline `python3 -c` one-liners, and none of it was kept. Names are clear enough (`wal_orig_path`, `unxored`, `encrypted_data`), but escaped multi-line inline scripts are hard to read and there are no docstrings or functions.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No decrypt or extract script is left to re-run. The diff holds only the modified binary `main.db-wal` and a generated `recovered.json`. The XOR logic is copy-pasted across steps 8, 11, 14, 21 and 23. This misses the project convention of a small re-runnable script.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: `b ^ 0x42` is hardcoded in the final write step and never derived in code. The final step shows no magic check after decryption and no error handling. Connections are closed and the result is checked afterwards, so nothing is silently swallowed.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: Checked the XOR'd header against magic 0x377f0682 and page size 4096. Parsed frame salts and commit markers. Let SQLite replay the WAL on test copies, ran `integrity_check` -> ok, checked the count of 11 and the column types, then validated the JSON.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: Step 1: `cp /app/main.db-wal /tmp/backup/main.db-wal.orig`, with main.db also backed up, before any change. All experiments ran on copies in /tmp, and `cmp` confirmed main.db was unchanged. The backup was removed only after recovery was verified.
